- Heatmaps and grid maps are always below `addGeoJSON` layers and markers. Clicking an `addGeoJSON` feature opens that feature's popup, not the popup of the cell underneath.
- Included in exports by [`exportMapImage`](maptools#exportmapimageid-responsefunction-options-and-downloadmapimageid-filename-responsefunction-options) in `maptools.js`. The legend is not, because map controls are not exported.
- Very large data (hundreds of thousands of points) still works, but send it as a `[lng, lat, value]` array instead of GeoJSON to save memory and parse faster.
- A heatmap shows **density** (where there are many points). To show a **value** at a place (for example signal strength), use `addGridMap` with `value` — a heatmap weighted by signal value would be misleading, because places with many measurements look "hot" even when the signal is weak.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/model3d

# `model3d.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../model3d)*

`model3d.js` displays **glTF 2.0** 3D models (`.glb` and `.gltf`) directly in the browser: rotate, zoom, click a part, change its color, hide it, or change its position and rotation from code. Everything is written from scratch on top of WebGL — its own GLB binary parser, matrices, shaders, and orbit controls — without Three.js (about 600 KB) or any other library. Its size is about 16 KB gzip.

It renders with **WebGL2**, and automatically falls back to **WebGL1** in older browsers. On-screen move/rotate gizmos, HTML labels pinned to the model, animation, exploded view, cross-sections, and `.glb` export live in the add-on module [`model3dtools.js`](model3dtools).

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { createViewer, loadModel } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/model3d.js";
```

## Minimal Example

```html
<!-- index.html -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<div id="model" class="model"></div>
<output id="status"></output>
<script type="module" src="index.js"></script>
```

```css
/* style.css — the viewer fills its element, so a height is required */
.model { height: 420px; }
```

```javascript
// index.js
import { createViewer, loadModel, onModelClick, highlightPart } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/model3d.js";
import { setInnerText } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

createViewer("model");
loadModel("model", "models/bts.glb", (info, error) => {
    if (!info) return setInnerText("status", "Gagal: " + error);
    setInnerText("status", `${info.parts.length} bagian, ${info.triangles} segitiga`);
});

onModelClick("model", (hit) => {
    highlightPart("model", hit ? hit.part : null);
    setInnerText("status", hit ? hit.path.join(" › ") : "—");
});
```

## `createViewer(id, options)`

Creates a viewer inside element `id` (usually a `<div>`). The element must have a height set from CSS. Calling it again with the same `id` recreates the viewer.

`options` (all optional):

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `background` | light gray gradient | Background, any CSS `background` value (`"#1a1a1a"`, a gradient, `"transparent"`) |
| `autoRotate` | `0` | Degrees per second the model spins on its own. Stops as soon as the user touches it |
| `fov` | `45` | Camera's vertical field of view, in degrees |
| `controls` | `true` | `false` = no user rotate/zoom/pan, e.g. for a static product view |
| `webgl` | `2` | `1` = force WebGL1, to test how it looks in older browsers |
| `dracoDecoder` | from `www.gstatic.com` | Folder of the Draco decoder (`draco_wasm_wrapper_gltf.js` + `draco_decoder_gltf.wasm`) for Draco-compressed models. Set it to your own folder if the app must not depend on Google's servers |

If the browser has no WebGL at all, the viewer shows a message and every other function does nothing.

## `loadModel(id, source, responseFunction)`

Loads a model, replacing the previous one. The camera is adjusted automatically so the whole model is visible.

- `source` — URL of a `.glb`/`.gltf` file, a **File/Blob** (e.g. from `<input type="file">`), or an `ArrayBuffer`.
- `responseFunction(info, error)` — called once the model is displayed. `info` contains:

| Key | Contents |
|---|---|
| `parts` | Names of all parts (nodes), in tree order |
| `triangles` | Number of triangles |
| `bounds` | `{ min, max, center, size }` the model's bounding box, in model units (glTF uses meters) |

On failure, `info` = `null` and `error` holds the reason (also printed to the console). `loadModel` also returns a Promise of the same `info`, so it can be `await`ed.

```javascript
// Opening a file from the user's computer
import { onChange } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

onChange("file", () => {
    loadModel("model", document.getElementById("file").files[0], (info, error) => {
        console.log(info || error);
    });
});
```

For a `.gltf` that uses separate `.bin` and image files, those files are downloaded from the same folder as the `.gltf` URL. From `<input type="file">`, only `.glb` or `.gltf` with embedded data can be opened, because the companion files are not selected along with it.

## Model Parts

A glTF model is built from nested **nodes** — e.g. `Menara` › `Sektor_1` › `Antena_1`. In this module nodes are called **parts**, and they are looked up by name (the node name, or its mesh name if the node is unnamed). Changes to a part (color, hiding, position) also apply to all parts beneath it. If several nodes share the same name, all of them change.

### `getParts(id)`

List of all parts, in tree order: `[{ name, mesh, parent, depth, visible }]`. `depth` = depth in the tree (0 = top level), useful for building an indented list.

### `setPartColor(id, name, color)`

Changes a part's color. `color`: any CSS color (`"#ff0000"`, `"red"`, `"rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)"`) or `[r, g, b, a]` in 0..1. Alpha below 1 makes it transparent. `null` = back to its original color. The new color replaces that part's texture. Returns `false` if the part does not exist.

### `setPartVisible(id, name, visible)`

Shows (`true`) or hides (`false`) a part.

### `highlightPart(id, name)`

Marks the currently selected part in blue. `null` = remove the highlight. Only one name is highlighted at a time.

### `getPartTransform(id, name)` and `setPartTransform(id, name, transform)`

A part's position, rotation, and scale **relative to its parent** — the same as the `translation`, `rotation`, and `scale` values in the glTF file.

`getPartTransform` returns:

| Key | Contents |
|---|---|
| `position` | `[x, y, z]` |
| `rotation` | `[x, y, z]` degrees, Euler in XYZ order (same as Blender and Three.js) |
| `quaternion` | `[x, y, z, w]` the same rotation |
| `scale` | `[x, y, z]` |

`setPartTransform` changes only what is given: `position`, `rotation` (`[x, y, z]` degrees, or a quaternion `[x, y, z, w]`), and `scale` (a number, or `[x, y, z]`).

```javascript
// Azimuth 150° and downtilt 6° for the sector 2 antenna. glTF's Y axis points up.
setPartTransform("model", "Sektor_2", { rotation: [0, -150, 0] });
setPartTransform("model", "Antena_2", { rotation: [6, 0, 0] });
```

## `onModelClick(id, runFunction)`

`runFunction(hit)` is called every time the model is clicked or tapped (rotating does not count as a click):

| Key | Contents |
|---|---|
| `part` | Name of the lowest part that was hit |
| `mesh` | Its mesh name, or `null` |
| `path` | Part names from the top down to `part`, e.g. `["BTS", "Menara", "Sektor_1", "Lengan_1", "Antena_1"]` — for selecting the group rather than its small piece |
| `position` | `[x, y, z]` the hit point, in model coordinates |
| `distance` | Distance from the camera |

`hit` = `null` if the background was clicked. Returns a `stop()` function.

## Camera

### `fitView(id, name)`

Smoothly moves the camera so the whole model fits on screen. With `name`, only that part; `name` may also be an array of names, e.g. `["Sektor_1", "Sektor_2", "Sektor_3"]`.

### `setCameraView(id, view, animate = true)` and `getCameraView(id)`

`view` = `{ yaw, pitch, distance, target }`, only what is given:

- `yaw` — angle around the model, in degrees. 0 = from the front (the +Z direction).
- `pitch` — angle from above, in degrees, -89 to 89.
- `distance` — distance from the camera to `target`, in model units.
- `target` — `[x, y, z]` the point being looked at.

`getCameraView` returns the same values. Save them and set them again to "bookmark" a viewpoint.

### `setAutoRotate(id, degreesPerSecond)`

Spins the model continuously; `0` = stop. It also stops as soon as the user touches the model.

## `clearModel(id)` and `removeViewer(id)`

`clearModel` removes the model but keeps the viewer. `removeViewer` removes the viewer along with its WebGL context; the element itself remains.

## Built-in Interactions

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Drag with the mouse or one finger | rotates the model |
| Right-click + drag, Shift/Ctrl + drag, or two-finger drag | pans the view |
| Mouse wheel / pinch | zoom |
| Double-click | centers the camera on that point and moves closer |
| Click / tap | `onModelClick` |
| Arrow keys (when the viewer has focus) | rotate by 10° |
| `+` / `-` (when the viewer has focus) | zoom |

Users who enable *reduce motion* in their system get camera moves without animation and no auto-rotation.

## glTF Support

| Supported | Not yet supported |
|---|---|
| `.glb` and `.gltf` (embedded buffer, `data:` URI, or a separate `.bin` file) | meshopt compression — re-export without compression |
| **Draco** compression (`KHR_draco_mesh_compression`), see the [Draco notes](#draco) | |
| Nested nodes with `matrix` or translation/rotation/scale | |
| ***Skinning*** — characters or organs whose surface bends to follow bones, up to 64 bones per mesh | More than 64 bones (or more than the GPU can handle) — shown in a rest pose, with a warning |
| Node animation, played with [`playAnimation`](model3dtools#getanimationsid-and-playanimationid-animation-options) in `model3dtools.js` | |
| Base color, color textures (PNG/JPEG), per-vertex color (`COLOR_0`) | Normal maps, *occlusion*, and metallic/roughness textures |
| `metallicFactor`, `roughnessFactor`, `emissiveFactor` | *Morph targets*, cameras and lights from the file |
| Transparent (`BLEND`) and cutout (`MASK`), double-sided | `KHR_texture_transform` and other material extensions |
| All accessor types (Float32, Int8/16, Uint8/16/32), interleaved data, sparse | |
| `KHR_materials_unlit`, `KHR_materials_emissive_strength`, `KHR_mesh_quantization` | |

### Draco

Draco-compressed models (many models from Sketchfab and from export tools that shrink files) are decoded with **Google's official decoder** in WebAssembly. That decoder (about 300 KB) is downloaded only when a model that uses it is loaded — pages with ordinary models download nothing extra. By default it comes from `www.gstatic.com`; for apps that must run without Google's servers, copy both decoder files to your own server and set the `dracoDecoder` option.

### Skinning

Skinned meshes are driven by their bones (glTF nodes), so animation from [`playAnimation`](model3dtools#getanimationsid-and-playanimationid-animation-options) or `setPartTransform` on a bone bends the surface directly. Clicks and bounding boxes (`fitView`, hotspots) use the bone-deformed positions.

The lighting is simple: sky/ground light plus one directional light that follows the camera, with shininess based on `roughness`. It is enough to see shape and color clearly, but it is not full PBR with environment maps like Three.js or `<model-viewer>`.

## Styling

| Class | Element |
|---|---|
| `.crootjs-3d` | The viewer (contains the canvas and overlay). Its default background is set here and can be overridden from the page's CSS |
| `.crootjs-3d-loading` | Added to `.crootjs-3d` while a model is loading, e.g. to show a *spinner* |
| `.crootjs-3d-dragging` | Added while the model is being rotated/panned |
| `canvas.crootjs-3d-canvas` | The WebGL canvas |
| `.crootjs-3d-overlay` | HTML layer above the canvas (where hotspots and gizmos go) |

## Writing Your Own Add-on

`createViewer` attaches a small interface to its element, in the `crootjs3d` property. That is how [`model3dtools.js`](model3dtools) works without importing `model3d.js` (which would load a second copy with a separate list of viewers).

| `crootjs3d` member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `root`, `canvas`, `overlay` | The viewer element, its canvas, and the HTML layer above it |
| `requestRender()` | Requests a redraw on the next frame |
| `onRender(runFunction)` | Called after every draw; returns `stop()` |
| `onModel(runFunction)` | Called every time the model is replaced or removed; returns `stop()` |
| `camera()` | `{ eye, target, forward, right, up, viewProj, fov, width, height }` |
| `toScreen([x, y, z])` | Model point → `[x, y, depth]` pixels on the canvas, or `null` if behind the camera |
| `rayAt([x, y])`, `raycast(origin, direction, skip?)` | A ray from the camera through a screen point, and the first surface hit: `{ node, t, position }` |
| `findParts(name)`, `isShown(node)`, `boundsOf(nodes)` | Nodes named `name`, whether they are shown, and their bounding box |
| `getTransform(node)`, `setTransform(node, transform)` | Same as `getPartTransform`/`setPartTransform`, for a single node |
| `getModel()` | The loaded model: `{ source: { json, buffers, images }, nodes, roots }` |
| `readAccessor(index)` | glTF accessor data: `{ array, size, componentType, normalized, count }` |
| `update()` | After a node's `translation`/`rotation`/`scale` is changed directly (e.g. by animation), recompute and redraw |
| `setClip(plane, cap)` | Clipping plane `[nx, ny, nz, w]` (points with `n·p + w > 0` are discarded) and the color of the cut surface; `null` = no clipping |
| `parseColor(color)` | CSS color → linear `[r, g, b, a]` |

## Notes

- **No WebGPU.** A second backend would double the module's size, while WebGL2 is already available in nearly every browser and WebGL1 covers the rest.
- Models from other domains must allow CORS. Files opened directly from disk (`file://`) cannot be `fetch`ed; run through a local server, or open the file with `<input type="file">`.
- glTF units are meters with the Y axis up. Models from CAD applications that use millimeters will appear 1000× larger — the camera still adjusts, but `position` and `bounds` are in those units.
- Clicks are computed on the CPU against every triangle. A million-triangle model takes about 1 ms per click; no problem for ordinary models.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/model3dtools

# `model3dtools.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../model3dtools)*

`model3dtools.js` is an add-on module for [`model3d.js`](model3d) with tools for apps that modify a model rather than just display it:

- **Hotspots** — HTML labels pinned to a point or part of the model that move with it as the model rotates, and dim when hidden behind it.
- **Gizmo** — move, rotate, and scale handles for changing a part directly on screen with a mouse or finger.
- **Animation** — plays the animations stored in the glTF file, with play/pause/scrub controls.
- **Exploded view** — spreads the model's parts away from their center, like an assembly drawing.
- **Cross-section** — slices the model with a plane to see its inside.
- **Measuring tool** — distances and angles directly on the model's surface.
- **AR** — opens the model in the room through the phone camera: inside the page (WebXR, Chrome on Android), or via Scene Viewer (Android) and AR Quick Look (iPhone).
- **GLB export** — saves the model with all its changes as a new `.glb` file.

The middle three suit learning materials well: anatomy, engines, buildings, lab equipment. This module is separate from `model3d.js` so pages that only display a model don't have to download it (about 8 KB gzip).

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { createViewer, loadModel } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/model3d.js";
import { addHotspot, enableTransform, getAnimations, playAnimation, explodeModel, addSection, measureModel, addARButton, getARLink, isARSupported, startAR, exportGLB, downloadGLB } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/model3dtools.js";
```

The viewer must already be created with `createViewer`. Hotspots and gizmos that refer to a part name need the model to be loaded, so call them inside `loadModel`'s `responseFunction`.

## `addHotspot(id, anchor, content, options)`

Pins an HTML element or text to the model.

- `anchor` — a **part name** (pinned to the center of that part, and follows it if the part is moved), or **`[x, y, z]`** model coordinates.
- `content` — a DOM element (moved on top of the viewer), or text.

`options` (all optional):

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `at` | `"center"` | `"top"` = center of that part's top side, good for a label above an object |
| `offset` | `[0, 0, 0]` | Extra offset in model units, e.g. `[0, 0.5, 0]` slightly above it |
| `occlude` | `true` | The label is dimmed (class `.crootjs-3d-hotspot-hidden`) when its point is hidden behind another part of the model. `false` = always clear |
| `onClick` | — | Function called when the label is clicked |
| `className` | — | Extra CSS class |

Returns a `remove()` function. The hotspot is also hidden when its part is hidden with `setPartVisible`.

```javascript
loadModel("model", "models/bts.glb", () => {
    addHotspot("model", "Antena_1", "Sektor 1 · 0°", { at: "top" });
    addHotspot("model", "Kabinet", "Kabinet BBU", { onClick: () => tampilkanDetail("Kabinet") });
    addHotspot("model", [0, 30, 0], "Puncak 30 m");
});
```

For a label whose content changes (e.g. a sensor reading), pass your own element and change its content any time — the hotspot does not need to be recreated:

```javascript
const nilai = document.createElement("span");
addHotspot("model", "Antena_1", nilai, { at: "top" });
nilai.textContent = "RSRP -87 dBm";
```

## `enableTransform(id, name, mode, onChange)`

Shows a gizmo on part `name` so it can be changed directly on screen. There is only one gizmo per viewer: calling it again moves the gizmo to another part.

| `mode` | Handles | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `"translate"` | Red/green/blue arrows for the X/Y/Z axes | Moves along that axis |
| `"rotate"` | Three rings | Rotates around that axis. Hold **Shift** for 15° steps |
| `"scale"` | Boxes at the axis ends, plus an orange box in the center | Scales one axis, or uniformly |

`onChange(info)` is called continuously while dragging, and once more on release. `info` is the same as [`getPartTransform`](model3d#getparttransformid-name-and-setparttransformid-name-transform) plus `part` (the part name) and `dragging` (`false` on the last call — the right moment to save to a server).

The move and rotate axes follow the part's **parent** axes, so they match the reported `position` and `rotation` values. The scale axes follow the part itself. While a handle is being dragged, the camera does not rotate.

Returns `{ setMode(mode), remove() }`. The gizmo disappears on its own when the model is replaced.

```javascript
let gizmo = null;

onModelClick("model", (hit) => {
    if (gizmo) gizmo.remove();
    gizmo = hit ? enableTransform("model", hit.part, "rotate", (info) => {
        if (!info.dragging) simpanKeServer(info.part, info.rotation);
    }) : null;
});

onClick("mode-geser", () => gizmo && gizmo.setMode("translate"));
```

## `getAnimations(id)` and `playAnimation(id, animation, options)`

`getAnimations` gives the list of animations in the model file: `[{ index, name, duration }]`, `duration` in seconds. A model without animations gives `[]`.

`playAnimation` plays an animation. `animation` = its name or index (default `0`, the first one).

`options` (all optional):

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `loop` | `true` | `false` = stop at the end |
| `speed` | `1` | Speed: `0.5` = half, `2` = double, negative = backwards |
| `autoplay` | `true` | `false` = prepared but not yet running, e.g. to be driven by a slider |
| `onUpdate` | — | Function `(time, duration)` every frame, e.g. to move a time slider |
| `onEnd` | — | Function called when the animation finishes (only with `loop: false`) |

Returns a controller:

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `play()`, `pause()` | Play and pause |
| `stop()` | Stops and returns the parts to their positions before the animation |
| `seek(seconds)` | Jumps to a given second, including while paused — for a time slider |
| `setSpeed(speed)`, `isPlaying()`, `time()`, `duration` | Speed, whether it is playing, current time, and the animation's length |

```javascript
loadModel("model", "models/mesin.glb", () => {
    const animasi = playAnimation("model", "Langkah_Hisap", {
        loop: false,
        onUpdate: (time) => setValue("waktu", time),
    });
    onInput("waktu", () => animasi.seek(Number(getValue("waktu"))));
});
```

What gets played is **node** motion (position, rotation, scale) with `STEP`, `LINEAR`, and `CUBICSPLINE` interpolation — enough for engines, gears, doors, assemblies, or orbiting planets. Animations that bend the surface (*skinning*, e.g. a walking character, and *morph targets*) are not yet supported: the bones move, but the surface stays still.

## `explodeModel(id, amount, options)`

Spreads the model's parts away from their center. `amount`: `0` = together (original positions), `1` = fully separated, values in between are allowed — good for a slider.

`options` (all optional):

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `part` | automatic | Name of the part whose **children** are separated. Default: the first level from the top that branches |
| `distance` | `1` | Distance multiplier. With `1`, at `amount` 1 each part's distance from the center doubles |
| `animate` | `true` | `false` = move instantly. Use `false` for values from a slider, so it follows the finger without lag |

Each part moves straight away from its group's center. Going back to `0` restores the original positions exactly; the positions at that moment also become the reference for the next separation.

```javascript
onInput("pisah", () => {
    explodeModel("model", Number(getValue("pisah")), { part: "Mesin", animate: false });
});
```

Animation, the gizmo, and the exploded view all change part positions. Return the exploded view to `0` before playing an animation or using the gizmo on the same parts.

## `addSection(id, options)`

Slices the model with a plane. The cut-away side is not drawn and cannot be clicked; the cut surface is filled with a flat color, so hollow objects look like solids split open. Hotspots whose points are cut away are hidden.

`options` (all optional):

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `axis` | `"x"` | `"x"` = vertical plane splitting left-right, `"z"` = vertical front-back, `"y"` = horizontal; or `[x, y, z]` the direction of a tilted plane |
| `position` | `0.5` | Position of the plane along that axis: `0` = the model's lower end (model whole), `1` = upper end (model gone) |
| `flip` | `false` | `true` = the opposite side is discarded |
| `color` | the part's color, darkened | CSS color of the cut surface, e.g. `"#facc15"` to make the slice stand out |

Only one section per viewer; calling again replaces the old one. Returns `{ set(options), remove() }` — `set` changes some of the options, e.g. from a slider:

```javascript
const potongan = addSection("model", { axis: "x", color: "#facc15" });
onInput("letak", () => potongan.set({ position: Number(getValue("letak")) }));
onClick("utuh", () => potongan.remove());
```

## `measureModel(id, options)`

A measuring tool on the model's surface (since 0.0.30): click or tap points on the model, and the lines and result appear on top of it and move with it as the model rotates. Clicks outside the model are ignored; a click after a measurement is complete starts a new one.

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `"distance"` | `"distance"`: two points → straight-line distance. `"angle"`: three points → the angle at the second point, e.g. a joint angle or the slope of a frame member |
| `scale` | `1` | Meters per model unit. glTF uses meters; set something else if the model was built to scale |
| `onChange` | — | `function (result)` each time a point is added |

`result` = `{ mode, points, distance, angle, text, complete }`: `distance` in meters (distance mode), `angle` in degrees (angle mode), `text` ready to display (`"12,5 cm"`, `"1,24 m"`, `"87,5°"`), and `complete` = `true` once all points are in place.

Returns `{ getResult(), clear(), remove() }`. Clicks are still passed on to `onModelClick` while measuring.

```javascript
import { onClick, setInnerText } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

let alat = null;
onClick("ukur-sudut", () => {
    if (alat) alat.remove();
    alat = measureModel("model", {
        mode: "angle",
        onChange: (hasil) => setInnerText("hasil", hasil.complete ? "Angle: " + hasil.text : "Click the next point"),
    });
});
```

## `addARButton(id, url, options)` and `getARLink(url, options)`

A **"Lihat di AR"** ("View in AR") button in the corner of the viewer: the model is placed in the real room through the phone camera, and can be moved and rotated with a finger.

| Device | What happens |
|---|---|
| Android | Opens **Scene Viewer** (Google's app) with the `url` file |
| iPhone/iPad | Opens **AR Quick Look** — only if `options.usdz` is set, because Quick Look cannot open `.glb`. Convert it to `.usdz` first (e.g. with Apple's Reality Converter) |
| Others (desktop) | The button is not added |

`url` must be a `.glb`/`.gltf` file publicly downloadable over HTTPS — not a local file or a `blob:` from `exportGLB`, because another app opens it.

`options` (all optional): `title` (title in Scene Viewer), `usdz` (file for iPhone/iPad), `label` (default "Lihat di AR"), `mode` (`"ar_preferred"` default, `"ar_only"`, `"3d_only"`), `fallback` (page to use if Scene Viewer is not available; default this page), and `webxr` (since 0.0.30): `true` = on devices that support it, AR opens **inside the page** with [`startAR`](#isarsupported-and-startarid-options) (the `startAR` options are used as well); on other devices it is still Scene Viewer/Quick Look.

Returns `{ supported, remove() }` — `supported` = `false` if the button was not added on this device.

`getARLink(url, options)` gives just the Scene Viewer link, for your own button or QR code.

```javascript
loadModel("model", "https://contoh.id/models/bts.glb", () => {
    addARButton("model", "https://contoh.id/models/bts.glb", { title: "Menara BTS", usdz: "https://contoh.id/models/bts.usdz" });
});
```

## `isARSupported()` and `startAR(id, options)`

AR **inside the page** via WebXR (since 0.0.30). The difference from Scene Viewer: the user does not switch apps, and the model shown is the model in the viewer as it is, including colors, hidden parts, and positions changed from code. That is also why it works for models from `blob:` or local files.

`isARSupported()` → Promise of `true` if the browser can open a WebXR AR session. Currently that is Chrome on Android with Google Play Services for AR (ARCore); Safari on iPhone does not support WebXR AR yet.

`startAR(id, options)` opens the model currently shown in viewer `id`:

1. The phone camera shows the room, and the model follows the floor/table being pointed at as a preview.
2. A tap places the model there; tap again to move it.
3. The **Tutup** ("Close") button ends AR.

The model is shown at its real size (glTF uses meters), with its base on the surface.

It must be called from a user click/tap; browsers refuse to open AR without one.

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `scale` | `1` | Size multiplier, e.g. `0.1` for a 30 m tower so it fits on a table |
| `hint` | "Arahkan kamera ke lantai, lalu ketuk untuk menaruh model." ("Point the camera at the floor, then tap to place the model.") | Instruction text above the camera view |
| `onPlace` | — | `function (position)` each time the model is placed |
| `onEnd` | — | `function ()` when AR is closed |

Returns a Promise of `{ supported, end() }`; `supported` = `false` (with the reason in the console) if the AR session could not be opened.

```javascript
import { isARSupported, startAR } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/model3dtools.js";
import { onClick, show } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

if (await isARSupported()) show("tombol-ar");
onClick("tombol-ar", () => startAR("model", { scale: 0.1 }));
```

Not yet available: a model shadow on the floor, lighting that adapts to the room, and moving/rotating the model with a finger inside AR. For those, Scene Viewer and Quick Look are still more complete.

## `exportGLB(id, responseFunction)` and `downloadGLB(id, filename, responseFunction)`

Assembles the currently displayed model into a single `.glb` file, with all its changes:

- position, rotation, and scale from the gizmo or `setPartTransform`;
- colors from `setPartColor` (that part gets a new material, so other parts using the same material are not changed);
- parts hidden with `setPartVisible` are removed from the scene;
- external buffers and textures of a `.gltf` model are packed into the single file.

`exportGLB` passes a `Blob` (type `model/gltf-binary`) to `responseFunction(blob)` and also returns it as a Promise — e.g. for uploading to a server. `downloadGLB` downloads it directly as `filename` (default `"model.glb"`). If there is no model yet, `blob` = `null`.

```javascript
onClick("unduh", () => downloadGLB("model", "bts-editan.glb"));

// or upload to a server
onClick("simpan", async () => {
    const form = new FormData();
    form.append("model", await exportGLB("model"), "bts.glb");
    fetch("https://contoh.server/api/model", { method: "POST", body: form });
});
```

The resulting file can be opened again with `loadModel`, in Blender, or in other glTF viewers.

## Styling

Everything can be overridden from the page's CSS without `!important`.

| Class | Element |
|---|---|
| `.crootjs-3d-hotspot` | Hotspot label. The blue dot below it is `::after` |
| `.crootjs-3d-hotspot-hidden` | A hotspot whose point is hidden by the model (default: dimmed) |
| `.crootjs-3d-hotspot-clickable` | A hotspot that has `onClick` |
| `a.crootjs-3d-ar` | The "Lihat di AR" button |
| `svg.crootjs-3d-measure`, `.crootjs-3d-measure-label` | The measuring tool's lines and points (orange), and its result box |
| `.crootjs-3d-xr` | The instruction layer and Tutup button over the camera view during `startAR` |
| `svg.crootjs-3d-gizmo` | The gizmo |
| `.crootjs-3d-gizmo-x`, `-y`, `-z`, `-all` | Color of each axis (via `color`), and the uniform-scale handle |
| `.crootjs-3d-gizmo-line`, `-knob`, `-hit` | The visible line/ring, the handle tip, and the click area wider than the line |

## Notes

- The gizmo and hotspots are drawn as SVG/HTML on top of the canvas, so they stay sharp and are easy to style, and the gizmo is always visible even when its part is hidden behind another.
- For a part name used by several nodes: the gizmo grabs the first one, the hotspot is pinned to the center of all of them.
- Export copies the original model data as-is; old meshes and materials that are no longer used stay in the file (still valid, just slightly larger).


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/geomeasure

# `geomeasure.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../geomeasure)*

`geomeasure.js` contains the calculations most often needed for geospatial data: distance, length, area, point-in-area, nearest point, radius circles, and transformation from local coordinate systems. They are all pure functions — no map, no DOM required — so they can be used with or without [`map.js`](map).

Positions are always `[lng, lat]` as in GeoJSON, and results are always in **meters** (or square meters).

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { getDistance, getArea, isInside, createAffineTransform } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/geomeasure.js";
```

Functions that accept `geojson` are as flexible as [`parseGeoJSON`](geo): a `FeatureCollection`, a single `Feature`, a single bare geometry, an array of them, or JSON text. The examples below use `data` from [contoh.geojson](https://github.com/petapedia/geojson/blob/main/contoh.geojson).

## `getDistance(from, to)`

The distance between two positions, following the curvature of the Earth.

```javascript
getDistance([106.8272, -6.1754], [107.6191, -6.9175]); // 120258.27... (Monas to Bandung's town square, about 120 km)
```

## `getLength(geojson)`

The length of all lines in the data. For polygons, the perimeter is counted (including hole edges). Points have no length.

```javascript
getLength({ type: "LineString", coordinates: [[107.60, -6.90], [107.61, -6.90], [107.61, -6.91]] }); // 2215.84...
getLength(data.features[0]); // 110.70... (perimeter of the Rektorat building)
```

## `getArea(geojson)`

The area of all polygons in the data, in square meters. Holes are subtracted. Points and lines have no area.

```javascript
getArea(data.features[0]); // 710.28... (Rektorat building)
getArea(data);             // 1980.88... (both buildings)
```

## `isInside(position, geojson)` and `getFeaturesAt(position, geojson)`

`isInside` answers `true`/`false`: whether the position lies inside any polygon in the data. `getFeaturesAt` returns the polygon features that contain it (an empty array if none), to find out *which polygon*.

```javascript
isInside([107.5761, -6.8735], data); // true
isInside([107.5759, -6.8736], data); // false (between the two buildings)

getFeaturesAt([107.5761, -6.8735], data).map((feature) => feature.properties.Gedung); // ["Auditorium"]
```

A point that falls inside a polygon's hole counts as outside that polygon.

## `getNearest(position, geojson)`

The point feature (`Point`/`MultiPoint`) closest to the position. Returns `{ feature, distance }`, or `null` if the data has no point features. Lines and polygons are not compared.

```javascript
const terdekat = getNearest([107.5761, -6.8735], data);
terdekat.feature.properties.Gedung; // "ULBI"
terdekat.distance;                  // 38.24...
```

## `createCircle(center, radius, steps = 64)`

Creates a circle-shaped polygon Feature centered at `center` with a radius of `radius` meters. GeoJSON has no notion of circles, so the result is a polygon with `steps` sides.

```javascript
const radiusPresensi = createCircle([107.575914, -6.8732098], 100); // 100 m circle
```

## `createAffineTransform(from, to)`

Creates an *affine* transformation (translate, rotate, scale, skew) from pairs of control points: the *i*-th point in `from` pairs with the *i*-th point in `to`, each `[x, y]`. Its purpose is converting local-system coordinates — a CAD grid, a building floor plan, the pixels of a scanned image — into `[lng, lat]`, and back.

It requires at least **3 non-collinear pairs**. More than 3 are fitted by least squares, so extra control points average out measurement errors.

Returns a function `transform([x, y])`, or `null` if there are too few control points, the counts don't match, or they are collinear. The function also has:

| Member | Content |
|---|---|
| `transform.inverse([x, y])` | The reverse direction: from the `to` system to the `from` system |
| `transform.error` | The mean (RMS) residual of the control points after transformation, in `to` units. For `[lng, lat]`, 0.00001° ≈ 1.1 m. A large value means a control point was mistyped |

```javascript
// Three survey markers with known project grid coordinates (meters) and lng/lat.
const grid = [[1000, 2000], [1500, 2000], [1000, 2400]];
const wgs84 = [[107.57520, -6.87410], [107.57974, -6.87407], [107.57517, -6.87048]];
const gridToWgs = createAffineTransform(grid, wgs84);

gridToWgs([1250, 2200]);                 // [lng, lat] of that grid point
gridToWgs.inverse([107.5775, -6.8723]);  // grid [x, y] from lng/lat
```

Converting an entire GeoJSON dataset from a CAD grid is just a matter of mapping each of its coordinates with `gridToWgs`. To place a floor plan image using control points, see `addImageOverlay` in [`maptools.js`](maptools).

An affine transform on `[lng, lat]` is accurate enough for district-sized areas (a few kilometers). For much larger regions, or data in an official projection such as UTM/TM-3, use the projection's formulas.

## Example: Location-Based Attendance

The most common combination: draw the radius, get the user's location, then check whether they are inside it.

```javascript
import { createMap, addGeoJSON, fitMap } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/map.js";
import { locateUser } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/mapcontrol.js";
import { createCircle, isInside, getDistance } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/geomeasure.js";

const kampus = [107.575914, -6.8732098];
const area = createCircle(kampus, 100);

createMap("peta");
addGeoJSON("peta", area);
fitMap("peta", area);

locateUser("peta", (lokasi) => {
    if (!lokasi) {
        console.log("Lokasi tidak didapat.");
        return;
    }
    if (isInside(lokasi.position, area)) {
        console.log("Di dalam area presensi.");
    } else {
        console.log(`Di luar area, ${Math.round(getDistance(lokasi.position, kampus))} m dari kampus.`);
    }
});
```

For areas that are not circular, replace `area` with the campus boundary polygon from your GeoJSON data; `isInside` works the same way.

## Notes

- All calculations treat the Earth as a sphere with a mean radius of 6,371,008.8 m — the same value Turf.js uses, so the numbers match Turf. The real Earth is slightly flattened, so results can be off by a few tenths of a percent from precise geodetic measurements. For distances and areas in everyday applications this is more than enough; for land boundaries or legal purposes, use proper surveying instruments.
- Device location has limited accuracy (see `accuracy` in [`mapcontrol.js`](mapcontrol)). For decisions like attendance, allow some tolerance: a point 5 m outside the boundary with 30 m accuracy is not necessarily truly outside.
- Data crossing the 180° meridian (antimeridian) is not handled specially.
- For routes along roads (not straight lines), see [`georoute.js`](georoute).


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/georoute

# `georoute.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../georoute)*

`georoute.js` finds the **shortest route along the lines in your own GeoJSON data** — roads, alleys, campus paths, building corridors. The route is computed in the browser: no routing service is called, no API key is needed, and it keeps working offline as long as the data is already loaded.

This module is pure computation. It doesn't need a map; the result is plain GeoJSON that can be drawn with [`map.js`](map) or used as-is to get the travel distance.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { findRoute } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/georoute.js";
```

All [`geomeasure.js`](geomeasure) functions (`getDistance`, `getLength`, `isInside`, and the rest) are also exported from `georoute.js`, so a page that computes routes only needs to import from here.

## `findRoute(from, to, geojson, options)`

Finds the shortest route from `from` to `to` (both `[lng, lat]`) along the `LineString` and `MultiLineString` geometries in `geojson`. Points and polygons in the data are ignored.

Returns a `Feature` with a `LineString` geometry and `properties.distance` holding the route length in meters — or `null` if the data has no lines, or the two points are not connected.

```javascript
const jalan = {
    type: "FeatureCollection",
    features: [
        { type: "Feature", properties: {}, geometry: { type: "LineString", coordinates: [[107.60, -6.90], [107.61, -6.90]] } },
        { type: "Feature", properties: {}, geometry: { type: "LineString", coordinates: [[107.61, -6.90], [107.61, -6.91]] } },
    ],
};

const rute = findRoute([107.604, -6.898], [107.612, -6.907], jalan);

rute.properties.distance;  // 1440.70... (meters)
rute.geometry.coordinates; // [[107.604, -6.9], [107.61, -6.9], [107.61, -6.907]]
```

In that example neither point lies exactly on a road. **`from` and `to` can be anywhere**: each is snapped to the nearest point on the nearest line, and the route starts and ends at those snapped points. So click coordinates or the user's location can be used directly.

## Drawing the Route on the Map

Since the result is a plain Feature, `addGeoJSON` can draw it directly:

```javascript
import { createMap, addGeoJSON, fitMap, getGeoJSON } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/map.js";
import { findRoute } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/georoute.js";

createMap("peta");

getGeoJSON("jalan.geojson", (response) => {
    if (!response.data) return;

    const rute = findRoute([107.575914, -6.8732098], [107.5772, -6.8752], response.data);
    if (!rute) {
        console.log("Kedua titik tidak terhubung.");
        return;
    }
    addGeoJSON("peta", rute, { style: { stroke: "#2563eb", strokeWidth: 5 } });
    fitMap("peta", rute);
    console.log(`Panjang rute: ${Math.round(rute.properties.distance)} m`);
});
```

A complete example with draggable A and B pins: [demo](https://croot.js.org/examples/geo/route/) · [source](https://github.com/crootjs/examples/tree/main/geo/route).

## Data Requirement: Lines Must Meet at the Same Coordinate

Two lines are considered connected **only if they share the same coordinate** — at their ends or in the middle of a line. This is how OpenStreetMap road data is structured: every intersection is a single point shared by the roads that meet there.

As a result:

- Two lines that merely **cross** without a shared point are not connected. This is intentional: a flyover and the road beneath it also cross on the map, yet you cannot pass from one to the other.
- Two lines whose ends are merely **close together** (common in hand-drawn data) are not connected.

For the second case there is the `precision` option: the number of decimal places used when comparing coordinates. The smaller the value, the more loosely two points are considered equal.

| `precision` | Points are considered equal if they are roughly within |
|---|---|
| `6` (default) | 11 cm |
| `5` | 1 m |
| `4` | 11 m |

```javascript
findRoute(from, to, jalanGambarTangan, { precision: 5 });
```

If `findRoute` returns `null` even though the lines look connected on the map, this is almost always the cause. The cleanest fix is still to correct the data: when drawing, make sure lines that meet really share a single point.

## Notes

- **All lines are treated as two-way**, and what is searched for is the **shortest distance** — not the fastest time. One-way streets, turn restrictions, and speeds are not taken into account. This module suits pedestrian paths, campus areas, or your own networks; it is not a replacement for vehicle navigation.
- `properties.distance` is the length along the lines, from the starting snapped point to the ending snapped point. The distance from the `from`/`to` you provided to their snapped points is not included; compute it with [`getDistance`](geomeasure) if needed (for example to tell the user "your point is 300 m from the nearest road").
- The network is rebuilt on every call. In testing, a road extract with 252 segments was computed in a few milliseconds and a network of 22,500 intersections in about 0.1 seconds on a laptop; phones are slower. For city-scale data, crop the data to the area you need.
- If you use OpenStreetMap data, include its attribution ("© OpenStreetMap contributors"); its license requires this for the data too, not only for map images.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/url

# `url.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../url)*

`url.js` contains short functions for reading parts of the current page's URL (protocol, host, path, query string, hash), changing the query string and hash, navigating to another page, and listening for hash changes. They all read or change `window.location`, so they only run in a browser.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { getQueryString, getHash, setHash, onHashChange } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/url.js";
```

## Summary

Example values in this table are for the URL `https://example.com:8080/class/lesson/ch1.html?user=102#exercise`.

| Function | Result / effect |
|---|---|
| `getProtocol()` | `"https"` |
| `getHost()` | `"example.com:8080"` |
| `fullPath()` | `"/class/lesson/ch1.html"` |
| `folderPath()` | `"/class/lesson/"` |
| `getPath()` | `"class/lesson/ch1.html"` |
| `getQueryString()` | Proxy: `getQueryString().user` → `"102"` |
| `getHash()` | `"exercise"` |
| `setQueryString(key, value)` | Changes the query string; the page reloads |
| `setHash(hashvalue)` | Changes the hash, without reloading |
| `redirect(URL)` | Navigates away; the Back button can't return to the current page |
| `onHashChange(runFunctionEvent)` | Calls a function every time the hash changes |

## `getProtocol()`

Returns the page's protocol without the colon, e.g. `"https"`, `"http"`, or `"file"`.

## `getHost()`

Returns the host name plus the port when the port is written in the URL, e.g. `"example.com"` or `"localhost:8080"`.

## `fullPath()`

Returns the URL path (`window.location.pathname`), starting with `/`, without the query string and hash. For example `"/class/lesson/ch1.html"`.

## `folderPath()`

Returns the path without the file name at its end, e.g. `"/class/lesson/ch1.html"` becomes `"/class/lesson/"`.

The last segment of the path is treated as a file name when it contains a dot (`.`):

| Path | Result |
|---|---|
| `/class/lesson/ch1.html` | `/class/lesson/` |
| `/js/app.min.js` | `/js/` |
| `/class/lesson/` | `/class/lesson/` (unchanged) |
| `/class/lesson` | `/class/lesson` (no dot, not treated as a file) |
| `/v1.2/page` | `/v1.2/page` (the dot is only in a folder name) |

Before 0.0.30, `/js/app.min.js` was unchanged and `/v1.2/page` became `/`.

## `getPath()`

Same as `fullPath()` without the leading `/`, e.g. `"class/lesson/ch1.html"`. On the root page the result is `""`.

## `getQueryString()`

Returns a Proxy over a `URLSearchParams` of the current query string, so parameters are read like object properties. Values are always strings, or `null` when the parameter is absent.

```javascript
import { getQueryString } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/url.js";

// URL: https://example.com/product.html?id=102&tab=reviews
const query = getQueryString();
const id = Number(query.id);  // 102
const tab = query.tab;        // "reviews"
const page = query.page;      // null
```

The Proxy is read-only in practice. Every property name is passed to `searchParams.get()`, so `URLSearchParams` methods such as `has()` or `forEach()` can't be used through it, and writing a property does not change the URL. Its contents also don't follow later URL changes; call `getQueryString()` again.

## `setQueryString(key, value)`

Sets or replaces one query string parameter, keeps the others, and writes the result to `window.location.search`. As a result the browser **reloads the page** with the new URL and adds a history entry. To change the URL without a reload, use `history.replaceState` or `history.pushState` directly.

```javascript
import { setQueryString } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/url.js";

setQueryString("category", "books"); // ...?category=books, page reloads
```

## `getHash()`

Returns the URL hash without the `#`, e.g. `"exercise"`. When the URL has no hash, the result is `""`.

## `setHash(hashvalue)`

Changes the URL hash to `hashvalue` (without `#`). The page does not reload. The browser adds a history entry, scrolls to the element whose `id` equals `hashvalue` if there is one, and fires a `hashchange` event when the value differs from the previous hash.

## `redirect(URL)`

Navigates to `URL` (absolute or relative) with `window.location.replace`. The current page is **replaced** in the history, not added, so the Back button does not return to it. Useful after logging out or after a form is submitted. For a normal link that can be undone with Back, use `window.location.href = URL`.

`URL` is not validated. Don't pass a value from the query string or user input straight into `redirect` without checking its destination, so your page can't be used to send people to another site.

```javascript
import { redirect } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/url.js";
import { deleteCookie } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/cookie.js";

deleteCookie("token");
redirect("/login.html");
```

## `onHashChange(runFunctionEvent)`

Registers `runFunctionEvent(event)` for the `hashchange` event on `window`. `event` is a `HashChangeEvent` with `oldURL` and `newURL`. The function is not called when the page first loads, only when the hash changes.

There is no way to remove this listener, and each call to `onHashChange` adds another one, so call it once.

```javascript
import { getHash, onHashChange } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/url.js";
import { renderHTML } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

function showPage() {
    renderHTML("content", `pages/${getHash() || "home"}.html`);
}

showPage();                // hash when the page opens
onHashChange(showPage);    // later hashes
```


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/validate

# `validate.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../validate)*

`validate.js` cleans up the contents of an `<input>` as the user types: it changes letter case, strips characters that aren't allowed, converts local phone numbers to the `62` format, and formats numbers as Rupiah. The functions don't reject input and don't show error messages — `input.value` is simply overwritten with the cleaned result. For form validation with a per-field error message, use [`form.js`](../form).

Every function takes an **input element** (not an ID) and returns nothing. That makes them a good fit for `onInput` from [`element.js`](element/), which calls the function with `event.target`.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { validateUserName, validateHouseNumber, validatePhoneNumber, formatRupiah } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/validate.js";
```

## `validateUserName(input)`

In order: converts to lowercase, removes all whitespace, then removes every character other than `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`, and `-`.

| Typed | Result |
|---|---|
| `Budi Santoso` | `budisantoso` |
| `user.name@01` | `username01` |
| `Andi_Pratama-2` | `andi_pratama-2` |

## `validateHouseNumber(input)`

Converts to uppercase, then removes every character other than `A-Z` and `0-9` — including spaces, `_`, `-`, `/`, and dots.

| Typed | Result |
|---|---|
| `12a` | `12A` |
| `Blok C-7` | `BLOKC7` |
| `No. 5/B` | `NO5B` |

## `validatePhoneNumber(input)`

Removes every non-digit character. If the result is longer than one digit and starts with `0`, that `0` is replaced with `62`.

| Typed | Result |
|---|---|
| `0812-3456-7890` | `6281234567890` |
| `+62 812 3456 7890` | `6281234567890` |
| `0` | `0` (a single digit is left as is) |

This function does not check the length of the number. The internal check in [`stp.js`](stp) that requires `62` followed by 9–15 digits is a different function and is not exported.

## `formatRupiah(input)`

Removes every character other than digits and commas, then shows the result with a `Rp. ` prefix and dots as thousands separators. The comma is the decimal separator; digits after it are not formatted.

The unformatted value (digits and comma only) is stored as a string in the input element's `data-value` attribute.

| Typed | `input.value` | `data-value` |
|---|---|---|
| `1500000` | `Rp. 1.500.000` | `1500000` |
| `2500,50` | `Rp. 2.500,50` | `2500,50` |

The `Rp. ` prefix is stripped again on the next call, so it is safe to attach to the `input` event. To calculate with the value, convert `data-value` to a number; if it contains a comma, replace it with a dot before `Number()`.

## Example

```html
<label for="uname">Username</label>
<input type="text" id="uname">

<label for="telepon">WhatsApp number</label>
<input type="tel" id="telepon">

<label for="harga">Price</label>
<input type="text" id="harga" inputmode="numeric">

<script type="module" src="script.js"></script>
```

```javascript
// script.js
import { validateUserName, validatePhoneNumber, formatRupiah } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/validate.js";
import { onInput } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

onInput("uname", validateUserName);
onInput("telepon", validatePhoneNumber);
onInput("harga", (input) => {
    formatRupiah(input);
    const price = Number(input.getAttribute("data-value").replace(",", "."));
    console.log(price); // 1500000 for "Rp. 1.500.000"
});
```

## Notes

- Because `input.value` is overwritten, the text cursor usually jumps to the end of the input whenever the value changes.
- Cleaning input in the browser is a convenience for the user. The backend must still validate the data it receives.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/websocket

# `websocket.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../websocket)*

`websocket.js` opens a WebSocket connection that sends an ID as soon as it connects, passes every incoming message to a callback, and provides small functions to send messages and close the connection. It suits servers that expect the client's first message to be the user's identity.

Things to know before using this module:

- The server URL **must** be Base64-encoded (`btoa("wss://...")`); the module decodes it with `atob()`.
- The module logs to the console: `connected and set id`, `socket error rejected`, `connection closed`, and `incoming message` for **every** incoming message.
- There is no automatic reconnect. When the connection drops, only the `connection closed` log appears.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { openWebSocketSetId, connectws, sendMessagetoWebSocket, closeWebSocket } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/websocket.js";
```

## `openWebSocketSetId(id, url_ws, onMessage)`

Checks that the browser supports WebSocket, then calls `connectws`. Returns a Promise that resolves with the `WebSocket` object once the connection is open and `id` has been sent.

If the browser doesn't support WebSocket, it calls `alert("Please Update Your browser to the latest version.")` and returns a Promise that rejects with `Error("WebSocket not supported")`.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| `id` | Sent as is with `send()` as the first message after the connection opens |
| `url_ws` | The WebSocket URL, Base64-encoded |
| `onMessage` | Optional. `function (data)` called with `event.data` for every incoming message. If omitted, the module calls `window.catcher(data)` if that function exists (legacy style); if neither exists, messages are ignored |

```javascript
import { openWebSocketSetId, sendMessagetoWebSocket, closeWebSocket } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/websocket.js";
import { onClick } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

const ws = await openWebSocketSetId("user-714240001", btoa("wss://chat.example.com/ws"), (data) => {
    const message = JSON.parse(data);
    console.log(message.from, message.text);
});

sendMessagetoWebSocket(JSON.stringify({ text: "Hello" }), ws);
onClick("logout", () => closeWebSocket(ws));
```

The Promise rejects (with the WebSocket `error` event) if the connection fails to open. Errors that happen after the connection is open are not reported to your code.

## `connectws(id, url_ws, onMessage)`

The function `openWebSocketSetId` uses to open the connection. Same parameters and return value, but without the browser support check (and without the `alert`). Use `openWebSocketSetId` unless you already know the browser supports WebSocket.

## `sendMessagetoWebSocket(msg, wsocket)`

Calls `wsocket.send(msg)` if `wsocket.readyState` is `OPEN`. If the connection isn't open yet or is already closed, the message is **dropped with no error and no log**.

`msg` is sent as is. Plain objects are not serialized (they would be sent as `"[object Object]"`), so convert them with `JSON.stringify()` first.

## `closeWebSocket(wsocket)`

Closes the connection with `wsocket.close()`. The function only skips the value `0`; if `wsocket` is `undefined` or `null`, it throws a `TypeError`.



---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/stp

# `stp.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../stp)*

`stp.js` contains three functions for a phone-number login flow: request an STP code to be sent to the user's number, verify it, and request it again. Each function sends a JSON `POST` to an endpoint that is **hard-coded in the module** and cannot be changed:

| Function | Endpoint | Body |
|---|---|---|
| `sendSTP` | `https://asia-southeast2-awangga.cloudfunctions.net/domyid/auth/login` | `{ phonenumber, captcha }` |
| `verifySTP` | `https://asia-southeast2-awangga.cloudfunctions.net/domyid/auth/verify` | `{ phonenumber, password }` |
| `resendSTP` | `https://asia-southeast2-awangga.cloudfunctions.net/domyid/auth/resend` | `{ phonenumber }` |

So this module is only useful for applications that use that backend. For your own backend, use [`postJSON`](api/) from `api.js`.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { sendSTP, verifySTP, resendSTP } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/stp.js";
```

## Shared Behavior

All three functions are `async` and return a Promise of the response body parsed from JSON. The Promise **rejects** (unlike `api.js`, which never throws) in these cases:

| Case | Error |
|---|---|
| `phoneNumber` is empty | `Phone number is required` |
| `phoneNumber` doesn't match `/^62\d{9,15}$/` (starts with `62`, then 9–15 digits, no spaces or `+`) | `Invalid phone number format. It should start with 62 and followed by 9 to 15 digits.` |
| HTTP status is not 2xx | `Failed to send STP` / `Failed to verify STP` / `Failed to resend STP`; the server's response body is not passed on |
| Network failure | `TypeError` from `fetch` |

The number check happens before the request is sent. To turn `08...` input into `628...` as the user types, use `validatePhoneNumber` from [`validate.js`](validate).

## `sendSTP(phoneNumber, captchaToken)`

Requests a code to be sent to `phoneNumber`. `captchaToken` is a CAPTCHA token checked by the backend; the module does not create it.

## `verifySTP(phoneNumber, password)`

Sends the code the user entered (`password`) for verification. The response content is entirely up to the backend.

## `resendSTP(phoneNumber)`

Requests the code to be sent to `phoneNumber` again.

## Example

```javascript
import { sendSTP, verifySTP } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/stp.js";
import { getValue, onClick } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

onClick("send-code", async () => {
    try {
        await sendSTP(getValue("phone"), getValue("captcha-token"));
        console.log("Code sent");
    } catch (err) {
        console.error(err.message);
    }
});

onClick("verify", async () => {
    try {
        const result = await verifySTP(getValue("phone"), getValue("code"));
        console.log(result);
    } catch (err) {
        console.error(err.message);
    }
});
```


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/useragent

# `useragent.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../useragent)*

`useragent.js` contains one function that guesses whether the page is opened on a mobile device, by matching `navigator.userAgent` against a regex. No third-party library is involved.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { isMobile } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/useragent.js";
```

## `isMobile()`

Returns `true` if `navigator.userAgent` contains any of `Android`, `webOS`, `iPhone`, `iPad`, `iPod`, `BlackBerry`, `IEMobile`, or `Opera Mini` (case-insensitive), and `false` otherwise. Takes no parameters.

```javascript
import { isMobile } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/useragent.js";
import { show, hide } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";

if (isMobile()) {
    show("open-app-button");
    hide("desktop-download-button");
}
```

## Notes

- iPads running iPadOS 13 or later use a desktop Safari (Mac) user agent by default, so `isMobile()` returns `false` on them.
- The user agent can be changed by the user or by browser extensions. Use the result only to adjust the interface, not for security. For layout, a CSS media query is usually the better tool.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/trace

# `trace.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../trace)*

`trace.js` contains one debugging helper: attach it as an event listener and it prints the clicked or touched element and its coordinates to the browser console. It only writes to the console — it doesn't store anything, doesn't send data anywhere, and returns nothing.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { tapClick } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/trace.js";
```

## `tapClick(event)`

For every event it prints `Elemen yang dipicu:` ("Triggered element") followed by `event.target`, then one of the following (the log labels are in Indonesian):

| Event type | What is printed |
|---|---|
| Touch event with at least one finger on the screen (`touchstart`, `touchmove`) | `Jumlah sentuhan aktif:` (number of active touches) and `Koordinat sentuhan pertama:` (`clientX`, `clientY` of `event.touches[0]`) |
| Mouse event (`click`, `mousedown`, ...) | `Koordinat klik:` (click coordinates: `clientX`, `clientY`) |
| Anything else, e.g. `touchend` (no fingers left on the screen) | Only the target element |

Coordinates are `clientX`/`clientY`, i.e. relative to the viewport, not to the page or the element.

```javascript
import { tapClick } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/trace.js";

document.addEventListener("click", tapClick);
document.addEventListener("touchstart", tapClick);
```

`touchmove` can be attached too, but it fires continuously while the finger moves and will flood the console. Remove the listeners (`removeEventListener`) when you're done debugging.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/image

# `image.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../image)*

Despite its name, `image.js` doesn't process images. It contains two functions for picking a random color, for example for an initials avatar background or a category marker.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { getRandomColor, getRandomColorName } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/image.js";
```

## `getRandomColor()`

Returns a 6-digit uppercase hex color string, for example `"#7A2B9C"`. Each digit is picked with `Math.random()`, so a color too light or too dark for the text on top of it can come up.

```javascript
import { getRandomColor } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/image.js";

document.getElementById("avatar").style.backgroundColor = getRandomColor();
```

## `getRandomColorName()`

Returns one random Tailwind CSS palette color name, **without** a prefix or shade. The list (22 names):

`yellow`, `violet`, `green`, `red`, `rose`, `pink`, `fuchsia`, `purple`, `indigo`, `blue`, `sky`, `cyan`, `teal`, `emerald`, `lime`, `amber`, `orange`, `stone`, `neutral`, `zinc`, `gray`, `slate`

Some of these names (e.g. `sky`, `emerald`, `zinc`) are not standard CSS color names, so don't use them directly as a `color` or `background-color` value. Build a Tailwind class name instead:

```javascript
import { getRandomColorName } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/image.js";

const color = getRandomColorName();
document.getElementById("category-label").classList.add(`bg-${color}-500`, "text-white");
```

A built Tailwind setup only generates classes written out in full in the source code, so classes assembled at runtime like this need to be added to the safelist.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/loading

# `loading.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../loading)*

`loading.js` has no functions. It exports one constant, `loading`: an HTML string containing an animated spinner `<svg>` (8 colored dots rotating around the center). Put that string into any element while an asynchronous task runs, then replace it with the real content when it's done.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { loading } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/loading.js";
```

## `loading`

| SVG property | Value |
|---|---|
| `id` | `loading` |
| `class` | `lds-microsoft` |
| `width` × `height` | `80px` × `80px` |
| `viewBox` | `0 0 100 100` |
| Dot colors | `#e15b64`, `#f47e60`, `#f8b26a`, `#abbd81`, `#849b87` |

The animation uses `<animateTransform>` (SMIL) inside the SVG: one full rotation every 1.5 seconds with `calcMode="spline"`, repeating indefinitely. No extra CSS or image file is needed.

```javascript
import { loading } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/loading.js";
import { setInner } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/element.js";
import { getJSON } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/api.js";

setInner("product-list", loading);

const { status, data } = await getJSON("https://api.example.com/products", null);
setInner("product-list", status === 200 ? `${data.length} products` : "Failed to load data");
```

## Notes

- Because `id="loading"` is fixed in the string, showing the spinner in two places at once puts a duplicate ID on the page. Select it by the `lds-microsoft` class if you need to style or remove it.
- The 80px size is set with `width`/`height` attributes; a CSS rule on `.lds-microsoft` can override it.
- A spinner that is only an image isn't announced by screen readers. Add status text, for example in an element with `aria-live="polite"`, if users need to know data is loading.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/en/mongo

# `mongo.js` Module Documentation

*[Bahasa Indonesia](../mongo)*

`mongo.js` is a small **browser** module for working with MongoDB `ObjectId` values on the client — no MongoDB driver and no database connection at all. It only contains string/date utility functions.

## Usage (Import)

```javascript
import { generateObjectId, getDateFromObjectId } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/mongo.js";
```

## `generateObjectId()`

Creates a 24-character string in the shape of a MongoDB `ObjectId` (8 hex characters of the timestamp in seconds + 16 random hex characters from `Math.random()`, not a counter like a real ObjectId), directly in the browser, without calling a server or the `mongodb` library.

```javascript
import { generateObjectId } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/mongo.js";

const id = generateObjectId();
console.log(id); // e.g. "65f1a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b"
```

## `getDateFromObjectId(stringID)`

Reads back the creation time embedded in the first 8 characters of an `ObjectId` and returns it as a `Date`.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `stringID` | `string` | ObjectId string (24 hex characters, or at least the first 8) |

```javascript
import { getDateFromObjectId } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/mongo.js";

const created = getDateFromObjectId("65f1a2b3c4d5e6f708192a3b");
console.log(created); // Date from the first 8 characters of the ObjectId
```

## Notes

- This module does **not** connect to MongoDB — it only creates/reads strings compatible with the MongoDB `ObjectId` format, useful on the frontend for a temporary ID before the data is sent to the backend.
- A real MongoDB connection (the `mongodb` driver, `MongoClient`, etc.) is **server-side (Node.js)** code and outside the scope of `crootjs/lib`.


---

Source: https://croot.js.org/docs/conventions

# CrootJS Coding Conventions

These rules are **mandatory** for any code built with CrootJS — whether written by hand or generated by an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, etc). They apply to CrootJS's own repos (`lib`, `docs`, `examples`, `crootjs.github.io`) and to any project that imports CrootJS.

## 1. Separate HTML, CSS, and JS into their own files

- No inline `<style>` blocks in HTML. CSS lives in its own `.css` file, linked with `<link rel="stylesheet" href="...">`.
- No inline `<script>` blocks with logic in HTML. JS lives in its own `.js` file.
- No inline `style="..."` attributes. Use a class name and define the rule in the CSS file.
- No inline event handler attributes (`onclick="..."`, `onchange="..."`, `oninput="..."`, etc). Attach listeners in JS with `addEventListener` (or CrootJS's `onClick`/`onChange`/`onInput` helpers from `element.js`).

A page should look like this:

```html
<!-- index.html -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
...
<button class="copy-btn">Copy</button>
...
<script type="module" src="script.js"></script>
```

```js
// script.js
document.querySelectorAll('.copy-btn').forEach(btn => {
    btn.addEventListener('click', () => { /* ... */ });
});
```

Not like this:

```html
<!-- don't -->
<style> .copy-btn { ... } </style>
<button style="color: blue" onclick="doThing()">Copy</button>
<script> function doThing() { ... } </script>
```

**One exception**: loading a third-party library from its own CDN (e.g. Lucide icons, SweetAlert2) via a plain `<script src="...">` tag is fine — that's an external dependency, not inline application logic.

## 2. JavaScript must be loaded as an ES module

Every `.js` file your page owns must be loaded with `type="module"`:

```html
<script type="module" src="script.js"></script>
```

Never as a plain classic script. This matches how CrootJS itself is distributed (`import { x } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@<version>/module.js"`) and keeps the whole page in strict-mode ES module scope — no accidental globals.

## 3. Import CrootJS from a pinned CDN version

```js
import { getJSON, postJSON } from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/crootjs/lib@0.0.31/api.js";
```

- Always pin an exact version tag (`@0.0.5`), never `@latest`, in committed code — `@latest` can silently change behavior under you.
- Import only the specific module files you actually use (`cookie.js`, `url.js`, ...), not the whole library, so the page only loads what it needs.

## 4. No AI slop

Code generated by an AI agent must be as deliberate as hand-written code. These rules are checked in review; breaking one is a reason to reject the change.

1. **Never invent an API.** Before calling any CrootJS function, check its name, parameter order, and options against [llms.txt](https://croot.js.org/llms.txt) or the module's docs page for the pinned version. If what you need does not exist, write it explicitly in your own code — don't guess an option and hope.
2. **Use what CrootJS already has.** `api.js` for requests, `element.js` for DOM by ID, `map.js` for maps, `model3d.js` for 3D, `toast.js` for notifications. Don't re-implement them, and don't add a library that duplicates them (Leaflet, Three.js, axios, jQuery).
3. **No dead weight.** No unused imports, variables, or functions; no commented-out code; no `TODO`/placeholder stubs; no "example" functions nobody calls; no files that aren't needed.
4. **Comments explain why, not what.** Don't narrate each line (`// get the value`, `// import CrootJS`). Comment the reason behind a non-obvious choice, in the same language as the rest of the project.
5. **No fake content.** No lorem ipsum in finished pages, no invented statistics, testimonials, or claims ("trusted by thousands of developers"). Sample data is labelled as sample data.
6. **Handle errors that can actually happen.** Follow each function's contract (e.g. `api.js` reports network failure as `status: 0`); don't wrap everything in `try/catch` that swallows errors, and don't add checks for states that cannot occur.
7. **Stay in scope.** Change only what the task needs. Don't rename, reformat, or restyle unrelated code; don't "improve" things nobody asked about.
8. **Real HTML, not div soup.** Buttons are `<button>`, inputs have `<label>`s, everything works with the keyboard and at phone width. No decoration that wasn't asked for (gradients, emoji, animations).
9. **Verify before saying "done".** Open the page through a local server, check the browser console has no errors, and try the feature — including at phone width and with touch if it's interactive. Say plainly what you did not test.
10. **Pin and minimise dependencies.** Exact version tags only (never `@latest`), and only the modules the page uses.

Quick check before handing work back: *Does every CrootJS call exist as written? Is every line used? Did I run it? Did I change anything I wasn't asked to?*

## Why

- **Maintainable**: a reviewer (human or AI) can look at one file at a time instead of untangling markup, styling, and behavior mashed together.
- **Cacheable**: separate `.css`/`.js` files are cached by the browser independently of the HTML that changes more often.
- **No build step required**: this works with plain `<link>`/`<script type="module">` tags — no bundler needed, consistent with CrootJS's zero-install philosophy.
- **AI-agent friendly**: a coding agent generating or editing a CrootJS page has one unambiguous place to put each kind of code, instead of guessing whether to inline it.

## For AI coding agents

If you (an AI agent) are building or editing a page that uses CrootJS, drop `CLAUDE.md` into the project root — Claude Code (and compatible agents that read a root instructions file) will pick these rules up automatically:

```sh
curl -o CLAUDE.md https://raw.githubusercontent.com/crootjs/lib/main/CLAUDE.md
```

Read it in a browser at [croot.js.org/lib/CLAUDE](https://croot.js.org/lib/CLAUDE).
